W7223133993.abstract: School feeding programs generate large volumes of plate waste, yet most decentralized programs cannot produce comparable and auditable measurements of what is served, consumed, and discarded. Existing research on food-waste measurement, waste valorization, and sustainability assessment has developed largely as separate streams. This study develops and documents an auditable four-layer framework that links standardized Edge AI computer-vision quantification of school meal plate waste with material characterization, a five-stream cascading bio-valorization pathway, and system-level evaluation, within Indonesia's Makan Bergizi Gratis (MBG) program. The quantitative, engineering based design covers 50 schools in East Java across five operational zones and 1,200 matched tray pairs, with image-based mass estimates validated against physical scale weights using R², MAE, and MAPE. Waste fractions are characterized through proximate and ultimate analysis and routed to biodiesel, hydroxyapatite, black soldier fly larvae bioconversion, anaerobic digestion, and biochar-compost. Life-cycle and techno economic assessments evaluate the system at a 10 ton/day regional scale. The analysis indicates that standardization at the data-acquisition stage improves downstream comparability and that measured fractions can be linked to differentiated recovery pathways. The numerical results are project reported, the sampling frame is limited to East Java, and the LCA and TEA outputs remain scenario dependent
W7223133993.title: Systemic Quantification And Cascading Biorefinery Engineering Of School Meal Plate Waste

W7223138764.abstract: Soil salinity is a major problem for agricultural productivity, adversely affecting plant growth, physiology, and biochemical performance. Malabar spinach ( Basella alba L. ), an important leafy vegetable with high nutritional value, is sensitive to salinity stress, leading to reduced yield and market quality. Developing sustainable strategies to mitigate these effects is essential for its cultivation in marginal soils. This study aimed to evaluate the individual and combined application of biochar and plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) in alleviating salt stress in B. alba . A greenhouse experiment was conducted using a completely randomized design with three factors: salinity (150 mM NaCl), biochar, and PGPR inoculation. Growth traits, biochemical attributes, ion homeostasis, and antioxidant enzyme activities were assessed. Results indicated that salinity significantly reduced non-enzymatic antioxidants (carotenoids, ascorbic acid, flavonoids, and phenolics) and elevated oxidative damage, as reflected by increased malondialdehyde (MDA). Proline accumulation increased as part of the osmotic adjustment response typical under salt stress. For example, 150 mM NaCl reduced plant height by approximately 36% and chlorophyll content by 30% compared with the control. The combined biochar + PGPR treatment improved plant height by 54% and chlorophyll levels by 39% relative to the salted control, while also lowering Na⁺ accumulation by 41%. Both amendments individually improved growth, RWC, K⁺/Na⁺ balance, and antioxidant enzyme activity under salinity, while the combined biochar + PGPR treatment produced the strongest recovery, showing the greatest improvements in pigment stability, ionic balance, and oxidative stress reduction. This work provides one of the first detailed evaluations of biochar–PGPR co-application in B. alba , demonstrating a practical biological strategy for improving crop tolerance in salt-affected systems.
W7223138764.title: Biochar and PGPR co-application mitigates salinity stress in Malabar spinach (Basella alba L.) by modulating growth, stress markers, and antioxidant defense

W7223140064.abstract: Biodegradable and compostable plastics (BCPs) are increasingly present in municipal organic waste streams, yet their effects on compost quality and subsequent soil–plant interactions remain insufficiently understood. This study evaluated municipal organic waste composts containing 0% (MOWC0), 1.43% (MOWC1; national average), and 2.86% (MOWC2; twice the national average) certified BCPs. Compost quality was assessed before application, followed by a six-week soil incubation and a four-week pot experiment with lettuce ( Lactuca sativa L.). The presence of BCPs did not compromise compost maturity, stability, regulatory compliance, or trace-element quality. During soil incubation, total organic carbon and nitrogen were only slightly affected, whereas microbial indicators showed clearer responses. MOWC2 increased cumulative soil respiration by 81% and 63% compared with MOWC0 and MOWC1, respectively, and increased the metabolic quotient by 97% relative to the unamended control. Dehydrogenase, laccase, tyrosinase, and N-acetyl-β-glucosaminidase activities were significantly affected by treatment, indicating that compost addition influenced both microbial oxidative metabolism and enzymatic processes related to N cycling, while microbial biomass nitrogen in MOWC2 was 21% higher than that of the control and more than fivefold higher than that of MOWC0. After lettuce cultivation, compost application increased soil total organic carbon by 16–20%, total nitrogen by 26–31%, dissolved organic carbon by 45–72%, total dissolved nitrogen by 48–83%, and Olsen phosphorus by 18–22% relative to the control. Lettuce shoot biomass increased in all amended soils, reaching a maximum increase of 26% in MOWC2, whereas root biomass and biomass allocation were unaffected. Leaf potassium increased by 28–44%, and no accumulation of potentially toxic elements was observed. Overall, certified BCP residues at realistic and moderately increased concentrations were compatible with industrial compost production and soil application. Composts retained their agronomic benefits, although the stronger microbial responses observed at the highest BCP content suggest that soil biological indicators may detect early BCP-related effects.

W7223142258.abstract: The resurgence of Cannabis sativa L. (industrial hemp) has great potential to support the robust circular economy systems suitable for sustainable agriculture development. Traditionally, industrial hemp has been largely produced for industrial and medicinal purposes. However, the crop suffered an unfair blanket ban during the greater part of the 20th century after it was classified as a drug crop. While it is true that some varieties are psychoactive, there exist other varieties with low tetrahydrocannabinol concentration ( less than 1%). Hemp exhibits several characteristics that support circularity. Of note are its biological characteristics, versatility and effective resource utilization. This review focuses on the role of industrial hemp in a circular economy. The crop has the potential for whole-plant utilization, high efficiency in utilization of production resources and environmental sustainability. It is a good source of biodegradable polymers, thus offering a crucial source of renewable energy alternatives to petroleum-based fuel, minimizing greenhouse gas emissions, pollution and unsustainable dependence on fossil resources. The crop requires less water, fertilizers and is highly adaptable to diverse environments, thus making it a crop perfectly suitable for climate-smart agriculture. It has considerable carbon sequestration potential, making it a good candidate crop for phytoremediation of contaminated soils. Hemp can contribute to rural development through employment creation and crop diversification. However, despite these benefits, several bottlenecks for its adoption persist including difficult licensing frameworks, inappropriate processing infrastructure and low consumer awareness that retard market uptake. Overall, there is still great potential of sustainable economic transformation.
W7223142258.title: The Dynamics of Industrial Hemp within Circular Economy Systems: A Review

W7223144053.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in agricultural soils involves antibiotic residues, resistant bacteria, intracellular and extracellular resistance genes, and mobile genetic elements. Sandy soils can facilitate off-site transport through rapid drainage and limited sorption, although mobility alone does not establish greater AMR proliferation or human exposure. This structured critical review evaluates straw-derived biochar as a risk-management amendment, distinguishing direct evidence from mechanistic inference. The literature reports biochar-associated outcomes ranging from increases or negligible changes for individual genes to substantial reductions approaching 90% in particular experimental systems. No pooled effect was calculated because studies differed in feedstock, production conditions, amendment rate, soil and analytical methods. Evidence is strongest for sorption of selected antibiotics, metal retention and altered contaminant transport. Suppression of horizontal gene transfer and consistent resistome modification remain context dependent. No universal optimum pyrolysis temperature is supported; performance depends on contaminant and soil properties, and aging can improve or weaken retention. Field evidence in sandy profiles remains limited, particularly for deep transport, groundwater connectivity and crop exposure. Straw-derived biochar therefore represents a conditional AMR-management option requiring target-specific characterisation and validation. Future studies should integrate contaminant mass balances, absolute and relative gene abundance, mobile-element markers, metagenomics, culture-based measurements and multi-year field monitoring.

W7223146238.abstract: Lodging is a major problem in the production of cereals and oilseed crops. It causes significant quality and yield losses through stem breakage or root failure. Silicon (Si) has been shown to play an important role in strengthening plant structure, improving stem rigidity, and reducing the risk of lodging. Recent studies have demonstrated that soil and foliar applications of silicon enhance cell wall lignification by increasing silica, lignin, and cellulose content in stem tissues. Silicon also improves water-use efficiency, modulates plant hormonal balance, and enhances nutrient uptake under both optimal and stress conditions. Silicon mitigates lodging caused by heavy nitrogen application and dense planting by maintaining the proper balance between vegetative growth and stem strength. Unlike earlier reviews, it combines insights from both conventional and nano-silicon research, emphasizing the interactions of Si with Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium, Calcium, and biochar. The review identifies knowledge gaps in Si bioavailability and transporter gene regulation, and, in place of a purely descriptive inventory of single-factor findings, proposes an integrative crop × genotype × environment × management framework as the organizing basis for the future of Si-based nutrient management and breeding programs to improve lodging resistance and sustainable yields.
W7223146238.title: Silicon-mediated lodging resistance in field crops: mechanisms, agronomic management, and environmental interactions

W7223146437.abstract: ABSTRACT Poly(3‐hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) is a biodegradable polymer with environmental advantages, although its industrial application is limited by high crystallinity, brittleness, and a narrow thermal processing window. PHB was plasticized with commercial glycerol tributyrate (GTB) and tailored mixtures of di‐ and tri‐butyric glycerol esters (GDB/GTB) obtained by glycerol esterification with butyric acid. PHB formulations containing 20 and 30 wt% plasticizer were prepared by melt mixing and thermo‐compression and characterized by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and tensile testing. GTB and GTB/GDB mixtures reduced melting (Tm) and crystallization (Tc) temperatures compared to neat PHB, enhancing chain mobility and processability. The GTB/GDB ratio had a negligible effect on Tm, whereas Tc increased at GTB contents above 80 wt%. Crystallinity increased with GTB addition, while mixed‐plasticizer systems showed similar crystallinity values. Thermal stability improved with increasing GTB content. Plasticizers reduced Young's modulus and tensile strength while increasing elongation at break. Increasing GTB proportion slightly reduced tensile strength, whereas elongation increased when GTB exceeded 90 wt%, with almost constant stiffness. Adjusting the GTB/GDB ratio is therefore an effective strategy to tailor the thermo‐mechanical performance and processability of PHB.

W7223147304.abstract: Wastewater treatment is essential for reducing environmental pollution and improving effluent quality. Conventional biological treatment technologies, including the Moving Bed Biofilm Reactor (MBBR) are widely used for organic pollutant removal; however, their performance depends on wastewater characteristics, biofilm development, and operating conditions. The present study evaluates the potential application of titanium dioxide (TiO₂)-modified rice husk biochar in an MBBR system for wastewater treatment. The proposed approach combines the adsorption properties of biochar with the potential photocatalytic activity of TiO₂ to enhance contaminant removal. A laboratory-scale reactor with a working volume of 15 L was used to investigate treatment performance under controlled operating conditions, with a conventional MBBR serving as the control. Wastewater samples were collected from selected sources including a sewage treatment plant, a milk-processing facility, and industrial sources. Treatment performance was assessed primarily through biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), chemical oxygen demand (COD), and total dissolved solids (TDS). The study also considered the influence of reactor configuration, carrier characteristics, aeration, sunlight exposure, and biofilm development on treatment performance. The principal evaluation outcomes are the comparative removal efficiencies of BOD, COD, and TDS in the conventional and TiO₂-modified biochar systems. This investigation provides a basis for assessing the practical applicability of TiO₂-modified biochar in hybrid biological treatment and for identifying the operational and material-related factors requiring further investigation. Further quantitative validation is necessary to establish the magnitude of performance improvement, material stability and suitability for practical wastewater treatment applications.

W7223149657.abstract: Chitosan (CS), a natural biodegradable polymer with excellent biocompatibility and abundant modifiable functional groups, has attracted considerable attention in drug delivery and biosensing applications. In this study, a multifunctional chitosan-based fluorescent composite (CS-1) was constructed by introducing a natural product-derived fluorescent moiety, enabling NH₄⁺ sensing and cantharidin incorporation. The resulting CS-1@cantharidin composite exhibited good fluorescence stability and a sensitive response toward NH₄⁺ under physiological pH conditions (7.0), with a linear detection range of 0–7 μM and a detection limit of 0.016 μM. The composite also showed good selectivity in the presence of various physiologically relevant ions and biomolecules. Furthermore, CS-1@cantharidin reduced TPC-1 thyroid cancer cell migration and decreased PCNA mRNA expression, as demonstrated by Transwell and qPCR analyses. These results indicate that CS-1@cantharidin integrates NH₄⁺ fluorescence sensing with cantharidin-loading capability in a biocompatible chitosan-based composite, providing a potential multifunctional platform for ionic microenvironment analysis and cancer-related applications.

W7223149904.abstract: This study evaluated the impacts of two types of biochar, namely, corn-stover and sawdust, on biogas yield and the removal of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) during the anaerobic digestion (AD) of chicken manure. Corn-stover biochar and sawdust biochar maintained the pH under neutral conditions, and simultaneously, effective hydrolysis, acidification, acetogenesis, and methanogenesis avoided excessive volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and free ammonia (FAN) inhibition, resulting in a 27.69% (corn-stover biochar) and 19.65% (sawdust biochar) increase in cumulative gas production. However, the low specific surface area of sawdust biochar was not conducive to the growth and reproduction of microorganisms, reducing the total number of microorganisms and thus enhancing the removal of macrolide and sulfonamide ARGs’ absolute abundance compared with corn-stover biochar. Microbial community analysis revealed that biochar addition enriched Methanosarcina (up to >96% relative abundance) and syntrophic bacteria such as Sphaerochaeta and Fastidiosipila , which facilitated methanogenesis and substrate degradation. Furthermore, structural equation models (SEMs) revealed that total ammonia nitrogen (TAN), pH, and FAN indirectly determine ARG abundance by influencing potential hosts and intI1 . This study can provide a theoretical basis for the application of these common biochars in enhancing the efficiency of chicken manure AD and reducing environmental ARGs.

W7223154902.abstract: Microplastic (MP) contamination in agricultural soils has emerged as a critical environmental concern, yet remains comparatively underexplored relative to aquatic systems. MPs can alter soil structure, reduce porosity, disrupt microbial functions, and impair nutrient cycling, while also acting as vectors for co-contaminants such as heavy metals and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). Biochar, a carbon-rich material produced through biomass pyrolysis, has gained increasing attention as a potential amendment for mitigating these impacts via reducing the mobility and bioavailability of MPs through adsorption, immobilization, and improvement of soil physicochemical properties. This review synthesizes peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025, retrieved from Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar using systematic keyword combinations, with emphasis on laboratory experiments and limited field-scale investigations. Comparative analysis indicates that biochar performance varies significantly with feedstock type, pyrolysis temperature, soil properties, and microplastic polymer characteristics, influencing its effectiveness under different environmental conditions. Particular attention is given to conventional biochars and engineered variants (e.g. magnetized and functionalized biochars) for their role in microplastic retention and soil function recovery. Despite promising laboratory-scale findings, major limitations persist, including inconsistent biochar performance under field conditions, limited long-term validation, and the absence of standardized protocols for microplastic detection in soils. These constraints highlight the need for integrated remediation approaches, robust experimental designs, and supfportive policy frameworks. This review identifies critical knowledge gaps and outlines future research priorities to support the development of sustainable and scalable biochar-based strategies for managing microplastic-contaminated agricultural soils.

W7223158651.abstract: Since the structural discovery of DNA's double helix, it transitioned from a genetic carrier to a cornerstone of programmable nanotechnology and materials science. However, while synthetic DNA with predesigned sequences has dominated DNA-based materials, biomass DNA, naturally derived from bulk biological resources, has emerged as a powerful large-scale engineering material. This review outlines biomass DNA-derived materials and their multifunctional applications, framed as a "Biomass DNA Tree," representing biomass resources as roots, duplexes as stems, and advanced materials as leaves. For example, we examine the transformation of biomass DNA into sophisticated 3D-crosslinked hydrogel matrices for (bio)engineering, and their further processing into recyclable bioplastics, which supports carbon neutrality. Furthermore, we highlight biomass DNA organogels and fibers, as well as its utilization for energy storage, including supercapacitors, batteries, and interphase layers. Beyond these core areas, the review highlights breakthroughs applying DNA as functional materials for catalysis, soft robotics, OLEDs, medical patches, neuromorphic devices, and photoconductors. By addressing challenges and providing perspectives on future opportunities, this review aims to catalyze the next generation of materials science, emphasizing the role of biomass DNA in advancing biopolymer-based applications.

W7223172056.abstract: Biochar is a carbon-rich material derived from the pyrolysis of biomass. It is drawing more attention for air pollutant control because of its low cost, abundant feedstocks, and environmental sustainability. This review examines the application of engineered biochar to control gaseous air pollutants. Meanwhile, the preparation and modification methods for engineered biochar, including pyrolysis, activation, acid–base treatments, amine functionalization, and metal loading, are also systematically summarized. These approaches are used for tailoring pore structural features and the distribution of surface functional groups. Moreover, the review clarifies the synergistic mechanisms of physisorption–chemisorption for CO2, SO2, NOx, and VOCs, emphasizing the cooperative regulation resulting from nitrogen-containing functional groups and metal sites. For example, nitrogen-modified biochar increased SO2 adsorption capacity from 78.9 mg/g for pristine biochar to 135 mg/g under mixed gas conditions, while Na2CO3-activated cattail-derived biochar achieved an n-hexane dynamic adsorption capacity of 1.00 g/g. Subsequently, this study comprehensively compared engineered biochar with conventional adsorbents, including activated carbon, zeolites, carbon molecular sieves, and metal–organic frameworks, considering gas-phase pollutant removal efficiency, removal cost, and operational difficulty of supporting equipment. Although biochar is slightly inferior to high-end commercial activated carbon in terms of adsorption performance, it can be modified to achieve a level comparable to that of activated carbon. As the raw materials for biochar are derived from waste, the cost is virtually zero, and the production cost is approximately 50–80% lower than that of commercial activated carbon. These results demonstrate the potential of engineered biochar as a low-cost, sustainable alternative for controlling industrial gaseous pollutants.

W7223173588.abstract: The MgO/ZnO/N-doped biochar is prepared using the waste building wooden template as the feedstock for Pb 2+ removal from wastewater, which is investigated in the fixed bed and fluidized bed systems. The characterization analysis exhibits that the MgO/ZnO/N-doped biochar has high surface area and nitrogen-containing functional groups, contributing to Pb 2+ removal from wastewater using the X-ray diffraction, fourier transform infrared spectroscopy and N₂ adsorption-desorption analyzer. The Pb 2+ adsorption behavior is investigated by the Pseudo-second order and Langmuir models with Pb 2+ adsorption amount of 296.45 mg/g and excellent reusability. Besides, the Pb 2+ can be quickly removed from wastewater in the fluidized bed system compared to the fixed bed system. The Pb 2+ adsorption mechanism includes surface complexation and electrostatic attraction, based on characterization analysis. The co-existing substances have little influence on Pb 2+ removal. Besides, the MgO/ZnO/N-doped biochar can be used as an extensive adsorbent for the removal of other pollutants from wastewater. The waste building wooden template is converted into an efficient MgO/ZnO/N-doped biochar for Pb 2+ wastewater treatment.

W7223173816.abstract: Heavy metal contamination of aquatic environments remains a major environmental challenge due to the persistence, toxicity, and bioaccumulative nature of metals such as Pb(II), Cd(II), Cr(VI), Hg(II), and As(V). Agricultural waste-derived nanoparticles have recently emerged as promising sustainable adsorbents because of their low cost, high surface area, tunable surface chemistry, and strong metal-binding capability. This review critically evaluates recent advances in the synthesis, characterization, adsorption performance, and removal mechanisms of nano-engineered adsorbents produced from agricultural residues including rice husk, sugarcane bagasse, coconut shell, corn stover, and banana peel. Comparative analysis demonstrates that nano-functionalization significantly enhances adsorption capacity, kinetics, selectivity, and regeneration efficiency compared with conventional adsorbents such as activated carbon and mineral sorbents. Among the most promising systems, magnetic biochar nanocomposites and chemically activated nano-biochars exhibit particularly high removal efficiencies for Pb(II), Cr(VI), Cd(II), and As(V), owing to synergistic mechanisms involving electrostatic attraction, ion exchange, surface complexation, pore filling, and redox interactions. The review further demonstrates that synthesis route strongly influences adsorbent performance, with pyrolysis, hydrothermal carbonization, chemical activation, co-precipitation, and microwave-assisted synthesis producing distinct surface properties and adsorption behaviors. Beyond batch adsorption studies, this review highlights the growing importance of continuous-flow fixed-bed systems and breakthrough modeling for evaluating practical scale-up potential. Dynamic adsorption models including Thomas, Adams-Bohart, and Yoon-Nelson are discussed as essential tools for predicting column performance and reactor design. Existing life-cycle assessment and techno-economic studies additionally indicate that agricultural waste-derived nano-adsorbents can provide lower carbon footprints and reduced treatment costs compared with many commercial materials, particularly when low-energy synthesis routes and recyclable magnetic systems are employed. Critical challenges remain regarding synthesis standardization, nanoparticle aggregation, regeneration stability, environmental safety, and long-term fate of released nanomaterials. Future research should prioritize pilot-scale continuous-flow applications, multi-contaminant wastewater systems, standardized adsorption protocols, integrated life-cycle and techno-economic assessment, and development of multifunctional recyclable nanocomposites. Overall, agricultural waste-derived nanoparticles demonstrate strong potential as scalable, environmentally sustainable, and economically viable materials for next-generation heavy metal remediation technologies.

W7223174118.abstract: Long-term faba bean (Vicia faba L.) monocropping degrades soil and promotes Fusarium wilt. Intercropping and nano-biochar (N-BC) can improve soil health and suppress soil-borne diseases. However, their combined effects on Fusarium wilt in faba bean remain unclear. This study assessed whether combining intercropping with N-BC could improve faba bean rhizosphere soil health and reduce Fusarium wilt under prolonged continuous cropping. A pot experiment was conducted to compare faba bean monocropping with faba bean-wheat intercropping under an unamended control, biochar (BC), and N-BC treatments. Fusarium wilt incidence and rhizosphere physicochemical and biological properties were assessed. Intercropping reduced disease incidence and disease index by 8.57%-34.53% and 8.32%-30.20%, respectively. Under intercropping, BC reduced these measures by 14.95% and 15.17% compared with the control. N-BC further reduced them by 50.02% and 54.74% compared with BC. The combined treatment increased soil water content, macroaggregate proportion, organic matter, dissolved organic carbon, ammonium nitrogen, nitrate nitrogen, available phosphorus, sucrase, urease, neutral phosphatase, catalase, and polyphenol oxidase. It decreased bulk density and benzoic, cinnamic, p-hydroxybenzoic, ferulic, and vanillic acids. These changes coincided with higher relative abundances of potentially beneficial bacteria, including Pseudomonas, and a lower relative abundance of Fusarium. Combining faba bean - wheat intercropping with N-BC amendment mitigated Fusarium wilt while improving rhizosphere soil structure, nutrient status, and enzyme activity, reducing phenolic acid accumulation, and reshaping microbial composition. These findings support a soil-health-based strategy for sustainable continuous cropping management.
W7223174118.title: Nano‐Biochar‐Assisted Intercropping Alleviates Fusarium Wilt of Faba Bean by Enhancing Rhizosphere Soil Health in Long‐Term Continuous Cropping Soil

W7223174532.abstract: A field experiment was conducted during the rabi seasons of 2024–25 and 2025–26 at Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK), Palem, Nagarkurnool, Telangana, to evaluate the integrated effects of the recommended fertiliser dose (RDF), biochar and sulphur on groundnut cv. TAG 24 grown on an Alfisol. The experiment comprised 13 treatments arranged in a randomised block design (RBD) with three replications, involving 75 and 100% RDF, biochar at 2 and 4 t ha⁻¹, and sulphur at 40 kg ha⁻¹, applied alone or in combinations. Pooled analysis revealed significant treatment effects on dry matter accumulation and yield, but not on the measured quality parameters. The highest pooled dry matter accumulation was recorded with 100% RDF + biochar at 4 t ha⁻¹ + sulphur at 40 kg ha⁻¹, with values of 2976.6, 4461.9 and 5114.7 kg ha⁻¹ at 30, 60 and 90 DAS, respectively. This treatment also recorded the highest haulm (3743.2 kg ha⁻¹), pod (2938.6 kg ha⁻¹) and kernel (1970.7 kg ha⁻¹) yields, which were not significantly different from those obtained with 100% RDF + biochar at 2 t ha⁻¹ + sulphur at 40 kg ha⁻¹ and 75% RDF + biochar at 4 t ha⁻¹ + sulphur at 40 kg ha⁻¹. Protein, oil and oleic acid contents were not significantly affected by the treatments, although 100% RDF + biochar at 4 t ha⁻¹ + sulphur at 40 kg ha⁻¹ recorded the highest numerical pooled values of 26.23%, 48.55% and 46.17%, respectively. The results indicate that integrating RDF with biochar and sulphur improved groundnut growth and yield under the conditions of the study, while quality parameters showed only numerical variation.

W7223174852.abstract: The production of sustainable polymer-based composites from agricultural waste has gained great attention due to the growing demand for lighter and stronger materials. In this study, alkali-treated CLSF (30 wt.%) was used as reinforcement in vinyl ester composites containing 0, 5, 10 and 15 wt.% cashew nutshell biochar, fabricated by hand lay-up followed by compression molding. The effect of biochar content on the tensile strength, flexural strength, impact strength, Shore D hardness, erosion resistance and microstructure of the vinyl ester composites was systematically evaluated by mechanical testing, erosion testing, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-Ray Diffraction (XRD). Biochar inclusion remarkably enhanced the properties of the composites when compared to the unfilled composite, depending on the optimum filler content. The composite containing 10 wt.% biochar showed the best flexural strength (31.88 MPa) and Shore D hardness (83.22), coupled with minimum erosion loss (0.021%), hence high stiffness and abrasion resistance. However, 5 wt.% biochar showed the best impact resistance, indicating effective energy absorption ability. SEM study showed enhanced filler distribution and fiber–matrix interface interaction for lower levels of biochar content, but higher amounts (15 wt.%) caused agglomeration of particles with the appearance of microvoids, resulting in reduced mechanical properties. X-ray diffraction showed that biochar addition leads to better structural ordering. In general, the obtained results clearly show that using 5–10 wt.% of cashew nutshell biochar increases multifunctional properties of coconut sheath fiber/vinyl ester composites.
W7223174852.title: Structure–Property Relationships of Cashew Nutshell Biochar/Coconut Leaf Sheath Fiber-Reinforced Vinyl Ester Composites: Mechanical and Erosion Performance

W7223176195.abstract: The shift toward sustainable materials has fuelled the exploration of renewable carbon approaches to bioplastics, combining biomass valorization, the use of carbon dioxide (CO2), and polymer architecture. This review focuses on the valorization of second-, third-, and fourth-generation biomass, such as lignocellulosic residues, algal systems and industrial waste streams, in the context of integrated biorefinery systems. The importance of advanced pretreatment technologies is critically reviewed, but pretreatment is the most energy-consuming and cost-dominant process in biomass conversion and is one of the major determinants of process feasibility. Moreover, CO2 is considered a substitute for carbon feedstock, with catalytic polymerization pathways and new monomer platforms being prioritized. The sustainability of CO₂-derived polymers, however, largely relies on the efficiency of carbon capture and the use of renewable energy since energy-consuming activation and processing may negate environmental advantages when fossil-based energy is employed. This review also provides a correlation between biorefinery-based precursors and the relationships between the structure and properties of polymers, including the influences of monomer composition, crystallinity and material architecture on mechanical performance, thermal stability, and biodegradability. A comparative study of biorefinery generations explains the trade-offs between the availability of feedstock, complexity of the process and economic viability. Altogether, this piece offers a critical, integrative framework, which connects the selection of feedstock, conversion technologies, and material design, which highlights the design of a scalable and sustainable bioplastic system. Carbon-neutral materials can be made only when the processes of capturing and converting CO₂ are driven by renewable energy sources because the fossil-based energy source can neutralize the advantages of the use of CO₂ in the environment.
W7223176195.title: Renewable carbon strategies for sustainable bioplastics integrating biomass valorization with carbon dioxide utilization and structural property relationships

W7223178113.abstract: This study combines low biochar loading with raster-path programming to control directional heat transport in extrusion-printed polymer composites. Here, bamboo-derived biochar was incorporated into thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) to manufacture B-TPU composite filaments and fused deposition modeling (FDM)-printed heat-spreading structures. Biochar incorporation increased thermal conductivity in both measured directions, with a markedly greater enhancement in the in-plane (IP) direction. At 7.5 wt% biochar, the IP thermal conductivity increased from 0.23 W m−1 K−1 for neat TPU (N-TPU) to 1.06 W m−1 K−1, whereas the through-plane (TP) value increased from 0.20 to 0.38 W m−1 K−1, producing an effective IP/TP ratio of 2.79. The directly controlled raster and layered architecture governed this effective anisotropy, with the morphology of the dispersed biochar providing an additional contribution to heat-transfer-path continuity. In arrow-shaped specimens, the [0°, 0°] configuration produced a lower heated-tail temperature and a higher distal-arrowhead temperature than the [90°, 90°] configuration after 240 s, demonstrating more effective longitudinal heat spreading. In the finned demonstration, the [0°, 0°] B-TPU structure showed a base-to-fin temperature difference of 15.9 °C, compared with 33.5 °C for N-TPU under the same conditions. Finite-element analysis captured the observed temperature ordering and linked component-scale heat spreading to the measured directional thermal properties. Biochar incorporation also increased the apparent tensile modulus while reducing tensile strength and failure strain, with the largest losses at 7.5 wt% biochar. These results establish a sustainable additive-manufacturing strategy that combines renewable carbon filler content and raster-path design to program directional heat propagation in lightweight, geometrically customizable TPU structures.

W7223179093.abstract: Abstract Electrochemical degradation of tetracycline (TC) using a mixed metal oxide (MMO) anode was investigated in the present study. The inefficiency of hydroxyl radicals for TC degradation was revealed by the minimal pollutant degradation observed in anodic oxidation and electro-Fenton processes. The addition of peroxymonosulfate (PMS) and peroxydisulfate (PDS) resulted in effective TC degradation, and PDS showed higher efficiency than PMS. The efficiency of the electrochemically activated PDS process was improved with the addition of iron-loaded biochar (FBC) as a catalyst; and the optimal efficiency of 78% was observed at the natural pH of a 100 ppm TC solution (pH 5.6), operated at 1 V, with 250 ppm PDS and 100 mg/L FBC. The process was effective over a wide pH range, from 3 to 9. In situ-generated sulfate radicals and singlet oxygen were found to be the predominant oxidants responsible for TC degradation, even in sewage, with 73.7% TC removal. The process also resulted in sewage disinfection, with a reduction in total coliforms from 1.48 × 1012 CFU/mL to 2.8 × 1011 CFU/mL, and in fecal coliforms from 6.9 × 1011 CFU/mL to 1.2 × 1011 CFU/mL, in addition to cell wall damage to nematodes and rotifers. Overall, electrochemical degradation is an effective approach for TC removal from aqueous media .
W7223179093.title: Electrochemically Generated Sulfate Radicals and Singlet Oxygen for Enhanced Tetracycline Degradation and Sewage Disinfection

W7223179161.abstract: The transition from petrochemical plastics to lower-impact materials requires more than substitution of fossil carbon with biomass. It requires production routes that integrate renewable feedstocks, efficient biocatalysis, controlled material properties, credible end-of-life performance and economically realistic downstream processing. This critical narrative review evaluates microbial routes to bioplastics with emphasis on polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs), direct biosynthesis of lactate-containing polyesters, and bacterial cellulose as a structurally distinct microbial polymer relevant to bioplastic applications. Literature published principally from 2000 to 9 August 2026 was examined, while earlier foundational work was retained when necessary to explain PHA enzymology and polymerisation. The strongest evidence base concerns PHA production, for which Cupriavidus necator, Pseudomonas spp., halophilic Halomonas spp., methanotrophs, autotrophs and mixed microbial cultures offer complementary advantages. Renewable carbon sources now extend from purified sugars to lignocellulosic hydrolysates, waste oils, crude glycerol, whey-derived sugars, food-waste carboxylates, algal biomass, methane and carbon dioxide. Yet feedstock "renewability" does not by itself guarantee environmental or economic superiority: pretreatment severity, inhibitor formation, nutrient requirements, gas-transfer demand, sterilisation, polymer recovery and solvent use can dominate process burdens. Synthetic biology has broadened monomer spectra and enabled lactate-based and other non-natural polyesters, but many demonstrations remain less mature than conventional PHA fermentation. Characterisation must therefore connect monomer composition and molecular mass with crystallinity, thermal transitions, mechanical behaviour, barrier performance and biodegradation under specified environments rather than relying on generic claims of biodegradability. Across the field, scale-up is constrained by feedstock heterogeneity, oxygen and mass transfer, product recovery, reproducible polymer quality and incomplete techno-economic and life-cycle evidence. Future progress will depend on integrated strain-process-material design, standardised reporting, low-impact recovery, continuous or non-sterile production where appropriate, and application-specific end-of-life testing. Microbial bioplastics are technically versatile, but their sustainability advantage is conditional and must be demonstrated at the level of the complete production and use system.
W7223179161.title: Microbial Production of Bioplastics from Renewable Carbon Sources: Synthesis, Characterisation and Future Perspectives

W7223179347.abstract: Pyrolysis-based valorization of sewage sludge (SS) is limited by the low surface area and elevated ecological risk of the resulting biochar. This study investigated ternary co-pyrolysis of arecanut husk (ANH), municipal SS, and red mud (RM) in a fixed-bed reactor under N2 and CO2 atmospheres at 500–600 °C, to increase biochar surface area, lower heavy-metal ecological risk, and enhance hydrogen production. ANH supplied a lignocellulosic meso-channel template and high volatile matter (65.8 wt%), while RM (Fe2O3 ≥ 62 wt%) catalyzed pore development and helped immobilize heavy metals originating from SS. At the optimum condition (15% RM, N2, 500 °C), biochar surface area reached 184.6 m2/g, 2.71 times greater than the pure-SS baseline (68.2 m2/g); CO2 activation at 600 °C increased this further to 224.8 m2/g. The Hakanson Ecological Risk Index fell from 495.4 (pure SS) to 98.6 at 15% RM, meeting the EU Biochar Certificate threshold (RI < 150) for unrestricted agricultural use. Under CO2 at 500 °C, hydrogen yield reached 10.42 mmol/g, while NH3 and SO2 emissions fell by 61.3% and 54.8%, respectively, relative to the pure-SS baseline. Multi-response desirability optimization identified 15% RM, N2, 500 °C as the overall optimum among the conditions tested (D = 0.847). To the authors’ knowledge, few studies have examined ternary co-pyrolysis systems combining agricultural, municipal, and industrial waste streams under both inert and CO2-assisted atmospheres; these findings show that red mud addition can simultaneously improve biochar porosity, reduce ecotoxicological risk, and enhance hydrogen co-production from a ternary waste-derived feedstock.

W7223180963.abstract: Phosphorus (P) remains a persistent nutritional constraint in agriculture despite the accumulation of substantial native and fertilizer-derived P reserves in many cultivated soils. This contradiction is particularly pronounced in hot arid regions, where crops frequently experience P deficiency despite the presence of appreciable total and residual soil P. This opinion paper argues that the central challenge is not simply P scarcity, but P accessibility, governed by the interaction of alkaline soil chemistry, calcium carbonate, low organic carbon, moisture limitation, restricted diffusion, and weak biological turnover. In calcareous soils, soluble orthophosphate may progressively enter calcium-associated pools, to precipitate rapidly with calcium carbonate or sorb onto mineral surfaces forming insoluble calcium phosphate compounds while carbon and water limitations restricting ion diffusion as well as constrain microbial mineralization and rhizosphere-mediated mobilization. Thus, the conventional strategy of repeatedly increasing soluble P inputs may enlarge soil P stocks without proportionately improving crop acquisition. We propose a conceptual shift from chemical saturation to ecological mobilization, supported by three complementary strategies: (i) biological acceleration through native phosphate-solubilizing microorganisms, root mediated organic acids and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi; (ii) rebuilding the organic and biological components of the P cycle through organic amendments, humic acids, biochar and adapted vegetation; and (iii) precision spatial and temporal synchronization of P supply with root activity and soil moisture. The paper further emphasizes that residual soil P is not a homogeneous reserve: its contribution depends on the balance between mineral stability, release kinetics, diffusion, biological transformation, and plant uptake. Future research should, therefore, move beyond static estimates of available P toward fraction-specific and process-oriented assessment of P accessibility. For hot arid agroecosystems, sustainable P management will require integrating fertilizer inputs with the biological and ecological processes that govern the mobilization and recycling of existing soil P reserves.
W7223180963.title: Soil phosphorus in arid agriculture: The riddle beneath our feet: Opinion Paper

W7223181548.abstract: Sericulture generates recurring lignocellulosic residues through the pruning and management of mulberry, castor, tasar and muga silkworm host plants. These residues are often underutilised, although some may serve as feedstocks for biochar and activated carbon production. This narrative review examines published evidence on the characteristics of host-plant residues, relevant thermochemical conversion routes, resultant carbon materials and their potential agricultural and environmental applications. Slow pyrolysis, fast pyrolysis, carbonisation, gasification and chemical activation are considered in relation to feedstock composition and processing conditions. Studies on mulberry and castor residues demonstrate biochar or activated carbon production, while investigations of selected tasar host-plant materials show adsorption and electrochemical applications. Reported effects include altered soil nutrient availability, water-holding capacity and contaminant adsorption, although findings depend on feedstock, processing temperature, activating agents and application conditions. For example, mulberry-stalk biochar has been examined in soil nutrient studies, whereas activated carbons derived from castor and Terminalia residues have been evaluated for wastewater treatment. Evidence is less extensive for muga host plants, and conversion studies cannot be assumed to establish benefits for silk production. Important research needs include comparative feedstock characterisation, controlled field trials, assessment of mulberry leaf and cocoon outcomes, and evaluation of processing costs and life-cycle performance. Biochar production therefore represents a plausible waste-valorisation pathway, but its agronomic and economic benefits require further host-plant-specific validation.

W7223182007.abstract: Investigations into atmospheric pressure plasma jet sources have been conducted using electrical, optical, and spectroscopic diagnostic methodologies. Polymers play an indispensable role across a diverse array of industrial sectors; nevertheless, their surface modification is essential for numerous applications. This study investigates how an atmospheric pressure plasma generated in argon facilitates the modification of polylactic acid surfaces, leading to alterations in wettability characteristics and modifications in chemical composition with respect to surface oxidation. The study findings indicated that plasma exposure improved the surface wettability of the polymer by as much as 38%, along with an increase of 45% in adhesion work. The mechanical properties of the material exhibited a subtle transformation, indicating that the polymer samples were not thermally damaged by plasma treatment. Exposure of PLA to plasma led to significant modifications in the oxygen-containing functional groups of the polymer, corroborated by both XPS measurements, where Pindex increased by 20%, and FTIR analysis, which showed an increase in HI of more than 200%. Moreover, our results emphasize the applicability of plasma technologies for the non-chemical treatment of polymeric materials in 3D printing applications.
W7223182007.title: Exploring the Ar-plasma treatment capabilities for enhancing PLA filament 3D printability

W7223183642.abstract: Abstract 3D printing biodegradable porous polylactic acid (PLA) scaffolds is a promising approach to bone repair and should meet certain mechanobiological requirements, which are affected by the internal microstructures. In this work, the bionic interstructures of scaffolds, comprehensively synthetically considering variable pore geometrical features: geometry parameters (pore shapes and arrangement) and porosity, were simulated and optimized by finite-element analysis. It was found that the cross-sectional structure with circular pore arrangement, spherical pore and gradient aperture distribution, and the longitudinal-section gradient structure with small-size pores on the top and large-size pores on the bottom, contributed the lowest maximum stress and may be the optimal model of scaffolds. Based on the optimized model structure, PLA scaffolds were fabricated by the 3D printing method of fused filament fabrication (FFF) to investigate in vitro degradation behavior and cell proliferation performance. It revealed that this scaffold possessed suitable in vitro degradability and good biocompatibility, which could satisfy the needs of real histological engineering bone substitution.

W7223185935.abstract: The flexural response of a fused filament fabrication (FFF) part depends on the polymer, on the mesostructure the toolpath builds from it, and on how that mesostructure is oriented to the bending load. This review examines these factors for polylactic acid (PLA), polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG) and acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) printed with planar and non-planar toolpaths, and how well finite-element models predict the result. Because the interlayer bond forms while the polymer cools, crystallinity, annealing, moisture, ageing and test temperature shift flexural strength and stiffness, in directions that differ between polymers and treatment windows. The toolpath is a primary mechanical variable, with effects that depend on the test conditions. Of 84 finite-element studies, 26 are compared quantitatively with a flexural experiment, 23 independently. Only 1 of those 26 treats curved-layer or non-planar deposition, and the shortfall lies in the small number of non-planar studies that predict a mechanical response, not in a lower standard of validation. None of the validated models makes the polymer constants depend on temperature, moisture or loading rate, or gives the bond between layers of one polymer its own interface law, leaving thermal, hygroscopic and time-dependent behaviour, with non-planar bending, as the clearest gaps.

W7223187168.abstract: Purpose This review presents a critical evaluation of bio-based and bio-enabled cementitious systems as solutions for lowering resource use and climate change impact without compromising performance. This study aims to review their components based on the processing of the components, their interaction with the matrix, the mechanical properties, durability performance and Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). Design/methodology/approach This research uses a structured narrative review methodology based on peer-reviewed sources from the Scopus database, which includes peer-reviewed English-language literature from the years 2005 to 2025. Data were categorized in terms of material type, manufacturing process, density and test age, mechanical and durability performance and LCA functional unit, system boundary, biogenic carbon handling, energy and water metrics. Findings What emerges is an inherent performance-functional property balance, rather than a universally superior material per se. Low-density materials made from hemp, straw, wood and cork possess excellent insulating capabilities, yet generally do not have structural properties. Surface-treated fibers, biochar and Microbial-Induced Carbonate Precipitation (MICP) improve crack prevention, transport resistance and self-healing after cracking; however, some environmental gains might be compromised due to the use of increased chemicals and additional energy requirements. Results obtained in the process of comparative LCA are very much dependent on the choice of the functional unit, system boundaries, considered lifetime, allocation and biogenic carbon assumptions. Originality/value This review integrates a taxonomy-based approach linking feedstock choice and processing approaches to performance, durability and environmental impacts. Evidence tables of three themes include processing of constituents, mechanical properties and durability data and LCA studies. Moreover, there is a cross-theme research agenda highlighting the processes involved in design, standardization and scaling up.

W7223187314.abstract: Rice is one of the world’s most important staple crops, but its processing generates substantial quantities of byproducts, including rice husk, bran, straw, and broken rice, which are often underutilized or disposed of through environmentally unsustainable practices. Despite being treated as waste, these byproducts are rich sources of dietary fiber, proteins, lipids, phenolic compounds, vitamins, minerals, and other bioactive constituents with significant potential for food and industrial applications. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of established and emerging approaches for the sustainable valorization of rice production and processing byproducts. Relevant published literature was reviewed to identify current utilization pathways, emerging technologies, associated limitations, and future opportunities. Established applications include livestock farming, biochar production, biofuel generation, brewing, and rice bran oil extraction. In addition, recent advances in value-added food applications are discussed, including supercritical carbon dioxide (SC-CO2)-based extraction and drying technologies, aerogel production, bioplastics, fermentation, and 3D printing. These emerging technologies enable the recovery of high-value functional compounds, improve nutritional quality, and facilitate the development of sustainable food ingredients, biodegradable packaging materials, and personalized food products. Overall, integrating advanced processing technologies into rice byproduct valorization offers a promising pathway toward a circular bioeconomy by reducing waste, enhancing resource efficiency, and creating high-value products for the food industry. Continued interdisciplinary research and industrial collaboration will be essential to accelerate commercialization and maximize the sustainable utilization of rice processing byproducts.
W7223187314.title: Emerging Advancements in Upcycling Rice Processing Byproducts

W7223187740.abstract: Microplastics and nanoplastics (MNPs) are emerging contaminants in stormwater runoff, posing potential ecological and human health risks. Bioretention systems offer promising nature-based stormwater treatment, yet their performance remains highly variable. Biochar, particularly post-processed biochar, has demonstrated strong potential for contaminant removal; however, its effects on MNP removal, leachate quality, and plant performance in green infrastructure remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the combined effects of untreated and thermal air-oxidated (hereinafter: treated) biochars and native vegetation ( Rudbeckia hirta ) on the removal of polystyrene MNPs (0.02, 0.2, and 1 μm) from synthetic stormwater runoff, leachate quality and plant performance in bioretention systems. Both biochars effectively removed nanoplastics during the early MNP-spiked storm events. Vegetation substantially reduced MNP leaching during subsequent simulated rainfall events, supported by the detection of microplastics within root tissues, indicating plant uptake. Vegetation also reduced nutrient leaching, with larger plants exhibiting more pronounced effects, highlighting the importance of enhancing plant growth for contaminant removal. Although treated biochar reduced total organic carbon leaching during initial spiking events, both biochars increased P, K, and S leaching. Overall, our findings demonstrate synergistic effects of biochar and vegetation in enhancing contaminant retention in bioretention systems, advancing green infrastructure design and sustainable stormwater management.
W7223187740.title: Synergistic effects of biochar and vegetation on microplastic and nanoplastic removal from stormwater runoff in bioretention systems

W7223188294.abstract: ABSTRACT Fibronectin is an important extracellular matrix glycoprotein that plays a key role in regulating cell behavior, including cell adhesion, migration, and proliferation. For this reason, preconditioning of biomaterials with fibronectin is commonly used to enhance cellular responses. Nevertheless, protein‐material interactions constitute a complex physicochemical phenomenon that strongly depends on the characteristics of the supporting substrate. In this work, fibronectin adsorption was studied on different polyester‐based supports widely used in biomedical applications (polylactic acid ‐PLA‐, poly (ε‐caprolactone) ‐PCL‐, a 1:1 blend of PLA and PCL ‐PLAPCL‐, and poly (lactic‐co‐glycolic acid) ‐PLGA‐). This direct comparison among commonly used biodegradable polyesters under identical adsorption and characterization conditions provides a coherent framework for assessing substrate‐dependent differences in fibronectin adsorption. Qualitative and quantitative analyses were performed after immersing the samples in fibronectin solutions at two concentrations (5 and 20 μg/mL). According to the results, fibronectin adopts a globular conformation upon adsorption onto the polymer surfaces. A higher affinity was observed for PLA and PLGA, where a greater amount of adsorbed fibronectin was detected. This behavior correlates with the hydrophilicity of the materials, as determined by surface tension measurements. Furthermore, materials conditioned with 20 μg/mL fibronectin exhibited a higher amount of adsorbed protein compared to those conditioned with 5 μg/mL.
W7223188294.title: Fibronectin Adsorption on Biodegradable Polyester Surfaces: A Comparative AFM and Quantitative Study

W7223190905.abstract: The recent development of additive manufacturing (AM) technology has enabled the design and fabrication of a new class of materials with unique properties, known as metamaterials. Metamaterials derive their special properties from their cellular architecture. Among the most promising applications of metamaterials is the development of lightweight structural metamaterial lattices, capable of exhibiting high strength, stiffness and energy absorption, at extremely low densities, performance that no other conventional composite can achieve. Plate-based lattices and honeycomb structures are the most promising lightweight architectures due to their high strengthto weight ratio and energy absorbing capacity. By fabricating these sutures with composite materials their abilities can be further enhanced by creating multifunctional metamaterial structures with self-sensing capabilities. This thesis investigates the mechanical performance of three metamaterial beams, one with face-centered cubic and two honeycomb lattice architecture, fabricated by Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) using polylactic acid reinforced with carbon nanotubes. The beams were tested under 3-point bending, and their mechanical response was recorded simultaneously with their piezoresistive response. A finite element analysis was performed, and the numerical results were compared with the experimental data. The experimental results showed that the honeycomb structures exhibited higher loadbearing capacity and apparent strength. All specimens failed suddenly, consistent with the brittle behavior of the PLA-dopped CNTs material. The piezoresistive response depended on deformation mechanism. The bending-dominated FCC beam showed an insignificant response in the elastic region, while the stretching-dominated honeycombs showed a significant decrease. A sudden step in the resistance of one honeycomb beam detected a localized damage, indicating that the structures are capable of self-sensing their damage state. The finite element analysis was reliable for the elastic response of the beams.

W7223201265.abstract: Abstract The valorization of organic waste streams into biodegradable polymers offers a sustainable alternative to petrochemical plastics while addressing environmental pollution. In this work, polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) were produced by a mixed phototrophic culture enriched in Rhodopseudomonas palustris using a complex carbon feedstock composed of medium-chain carboxylic acids (MCCAs) derived from winery residues. Under nutrient-limited and alkaline conditions, a maximum biomass concentration of 1617 ± 17 mg L–1 was obtained in the batch cultivation, with a PHA recovery yield of 41.45 ± 3.5% from independent extractions of the recovered biomass. Comprehensive physicochemical characterization revealed a multicomponent PHA comprising 3-hydroxybutyrate (78 mol %), 4-hydroxybutyrate (5 mol %), 3-hydroxyvalerate (10 mol %), and 3-hydroxyhexanoate (7 mol %). Notably, 1H and 13C NMR spectroscopy provided structural evidence for 3-hydroxyhexanoate incorporation, which had not been identified in previous GC-based analyses of PHAs produced using the same inoculum and substrate system, highlighting the value of complementary spectroscopic approaches for resolving complex PHA compositions. Thermal and X-ray diffraction analyses demonstrated a semicrystalline structure, while dual melting transitions at 136 and 164 °C were consistent with heterogeneous chain architecture. These results demonstrate that waste-derived MCCAs can be directly assimilated into PHA backbones by phototrophic mixed cultures, expanding the compositional diversity of biopolymers accessible from environmental feedstocks. This work establishes a direct link among waste-stream composition, microbial metabolism, and PHA structure while advancing integrated strategies for circular biopolymer production.

W7223205939.abstract: Effective sludge dewatering remains a critical challenge in wastewater treatment due to the complex structure of extracellular polymeric substances that encapsulate bound water. This study investigated the synergistic effects of ultrasound combined with modified corn-core powder and sludge-based biochar on municipal sludge dewaterability. Orthogonal and single-factor experiments were designed to optimize conditioning parameters, and the underlying mechanisms were elucidated through comprehensive analyses of extracellular polymeric substance composition, three-dimensional excitation-emission matrix fluorescence spectroscopy, fluorescence regional integration, fractal dimension, particle-size distribution, and statistical correlation. The results demonstrated that optimal dewatering performance was achieved at an ultrasonic specific energy of 4000 kJ/kg dry solids for the modified corn-core powder and sludge-based biochar with ultrasound system, where net sludge solids yield increased by 124%, while specific resistance of filtration and moisture content decreased by 78% and 19%, respectively. Mechanistic analysis revealed that low-intensity ultrasound disrupted sludge flocs, released extracellular polymeric substance-bound organic matter, and promoted the shift of organic components from soluble extracellular polymeric substances to tightly bound extracellular polymeric substances, facilitated by the long-chain adsorption of modified corn-core powder and the skeleton-building effect of sludge-based biochar. Excessive ultrasound (specific energy > 8000 kJ/kg dry solids) caused particle fragmentation, increased system viscosity, and deteriorated dewaterability. Pearson correlation and principal component analysis confirmed that ultrasonic specific energy and organic components in soluble extracellular polymeric substances were the dominant factors governing dewatering performance. This study provides a promising strategy for reducing chemical conditioner consumption while enhancing sludge dewaterability through controlled ultrasound assistance.

W7223221368.abstract: This study investigated biochar production from stranded Sargassum biomass and its effects on lettuce (Lactuca sativa L.) growth and foliar elemental composition. Biochars were produced by laboratory-scale pyrolysis at 400, 500, and 600 °C and using an artisanal double-drum kiln. The resulting materials were alkaline and mineral-rich, with ash contents of 24.6–42.3 wt% and pH values of 8.4–8.7. Scanning electron microscopy coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM/EDS) revealed structural changes after pyrolysis, including the development of rough, porous surfaces. The SEM/EDS semiquantitative analysis indicated relatively high proportions of Na (4.55 wt%), K (4.31 wt%), Ca (2.46 wt%), and Mg (1.75 wt%) in the double-drum biochar, consistent with the mineral-rich composition of the original marine biomass. Lettuce responses varied with biochar application rate. Lettuce response depended strongly on biochar application rate. The 1 t ha−1 rate did not significantly affect plant growth, whereas 12 t ha−1 reduced shoot fresh mass by approximately 45% and decreased plant diameter, rosette diameter, leaf number, and leaf area. Foliar Na concentration increased from 4.95 in the control to 11.50 mg kg−1 at 12 t ha−1, while the Na/K ratio increased from 3.88 to 9.91. The highest application rate was therefore characterized by increased foliar Na and Na/K ratio together with reduced plant growth. These findings highlight the potential of Sargassum-derived biochar for biomass valorization and mineral recovery, while indicating that its high sodium content warrants careful consideration of application rates for lettuce cultivation.
W7223221368.title: Sargassum-Derived Biochar Affects Lettuce Growth and Promotes Sodium Accumulation in Plant Tissues

W7223226473.abstract: Recycled nutrient fertilizers (RNFs) derived from organic and industrial waste streams offer a promising approach to nutrient recovery and sustainable agricultural production. However, their agronomic performance and the potential benefits of enrichment with biologically active, waste-derived materials remain insufficiently understood. This study evaluated two multi-component RNFs, four-ingredient pellets, first with biochar (BADSS) and second with bovine shavings (SADSS), with and without enrichment using chitosan-containing seafood waste, in a four-month greenhouse experiment with ryegrass across nitrogen application rates ranging from 20 to 370 kg N ha−1. Biomass production, nitrogen uptake, agronomic effectiveness (AE), apparent nitrogen recovery (ANR), soil chemical properties, and photosystem II efficiency were assessed. The results demonstrated that fertilizer performance depended strongly on matrix composition and nitrogen application rate. BADSS induced a stronger increase in residual soil pH, whereas SADSS maintained more balanced soil conditions. Chitosan enrichment enhanced long-term nitrogen uptake and biomass production when combined with SADSS, while its effects in the BADSS matrix were less consistent, particularly at excessive nitrogen inputs. Correcting fertilizer performance for additional nitrogen introduced with the chitosan-containing amendment substantially reduced apparent AE and ANR, highlighting the importance of complete nutrient accounting when assessing enriched fertilizers. Overall, the findings indicate that seafood-waste-derived chitosan can improve the agronomic performance of recycled nutrient fertilizers, although its effectiveness depends on the composition of the fertilizer matrix and the applied nitrogen rate. Integrating seafood-processing residues into waste-derived fertilizer systems offers a promising strategy for valorizing underutilized resources, improving nutrient management, and supporting circular bioeconomy approaches to sustainable agriculture.
W7223226473.title: Agronomic Performance of Pelleted Multi-Ingredient Organic-Mineral Recycled Nutrient Fertilizers, Enhanced with Seafood-Waste-Containing Chitosan

W7223231513.abstract: Conventional low-density poly(ethylene) (LDPE) agricultural mulch films generate persistent plastic waste, which has motivated the development of biodegradable mulch films (BDMs) that can provide adequate performance during use while offering improved end-of-life options. Here, composite films containing poly(lactic acid) (PLA), poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT), microcrystalline cellulose (MCC), and hydroxyapatite (HA) were evaluated for their material properties and suitability as agricultural mulches. Correlation analysis and Elastic Net regression were used to examine composition–property relationships. PBAT primarily governed ductility and tensile performance, whereas MCC significantly increased water absorption because of its hydrophilic character. Water absorption was the most reliably modeled response (training R2 = 0.893), while mechanical property models showed limited validation performance, which indicates that composition alone could not fully predict unseen formulations. Several formulations met commercial BDM mechanical requirements. Multi-objective optimization predicted a composition of 9.3/80.7/3.5/6.5 wt% PLA/PBAT/MCC/HA. The combined experimental and modeling framework clarifies composition–property relationships in biodegradable polymer composites and demonstrates how data-driven approaches can guide the formulation of biodegradable agricultural mulch films.
W7223231513.title: Data-Driven Design of PLA/PBAT/MCC/HA Composites for Biodegradable Mulch Films

W7223232044.abstract: ABSTRACT Driven by the increasing severity of plastic pollution, biodegradable polymers such as poly(propylene carbonate) (PPC), owing to their biodegradability, gas barrier properties, and CO 2 ‐fixing capability, have attracted considerable attention as alternatives to conventional plastics. In this work, PPC/poly(butylene adipate‐co‐terephthalate) (PBAT)/epoxidized soybean oil (ESO) composite foams were successfully fabricated via an environmentally friendly supercritical CO 2 foaming process. The results demonstrate that ESO, acting as a reactive compatibilizer, forms chemical linkages between PPC and PBAT through epoxy ring‐opening reactions, significantly improving interfacial compatibility. The foaming performance of the composite system is enhanced, and the expansion ratio is markedly increased, reaching approximately 40.46 under the optimized formulation. In addition, the open‐cell structure and increased ester bond content substantially accelerate the degradation rate, with a mass loss of 57.96% within 26 days. The thermal conductivity of the foam is reduced to 32.46 mW m −1 K −1 , indicating excellent thermal insulation performance. This study provides a feasible strategy for developing lightweight degradable polymer foams with a desirable combination of foaming performance, degradation behavior, and thermal insulation properties.

W7223244670.abstract: Sustainable management of organic inputs is critical for improving carbon and nutrient stabilization while reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from biomass-based waste management systems. Composting offers a practical pathway for stabilizing organic amendments, but gaseous losses of carbon and nitrogen during decomposition can reduce its environmental and agronomic value. This pilot-scale study evaluated whether phase-specific application of Tithonia diversifolia in biochar-amended composting systems could improve nutrient contents and mitigate GHG emissions under tropical conditions. Four treatments were tested with three replicates: cattle manure + T. diversifolia + biochar (CMBT), cattle manure + T. diversifolia + maize stover (CMTM), cattle manure + biochar with T. diversifolia applied at day 70 (CMBT70), and cattle manure alone (CM). Compost quality and GHG fluxes, including methane (CH₄), nitrous oxide (N₂O), and carbon dioxide (CO₂), were monitored throughout the composting process. Cumulative greenhouse gas fluxes ranged from 36.11 g CH₄–C m⁻² (361.1 kg CH₄–C ha⁻¹) from the CMBT70 treatment to 67.44 g CH₄–C m⁻² (674.4 kg CH₄–C ha⁻¹) from the CMBT treatment, 1.40 kg CO₂–C m⁻² (14.0 t CO₂–C ha⁻¹) from the CM treatment to 1.99 kg CO₂–C m⁻² (19.9 t CO₂–C ha⁻¹) from the CMTM treatment, and 1.26 g N₂O–N m⁻² (12.6 kg N₂O–N ha⁻¹) from the CMBT70 treatment to 7.06 g N₂O–N m⁻² (70.6 kg N₂O–N ha⁻¹) from the CMBT treatment for CH₄, CO₂, and N₂O fluxes, respectively. Post-thermophilic application of T. diversifolia significantly improved total nitrogen (2.47%) and potassium (3.06%) concentrations at maturity, while reducing cumulative CH₄ and N₂O emissions by 46.4% and 82.2%, respectively, compared to CMBT. In contrast, biochar and T. diversifolia added at the onset of composting resulted in the highest cumulative GHG emissions and global warming potential, likely due to increased availability of labile substrate and transient anaerobic conditions. These findings indicated that phase-specific management of organic amendments can improve nutrient retention, enhance biomass stabilization, and reduce emissions from biochar-amended composting systems. This approach offers a low-input strategy to improve the environmental performance of organic waste valorization and circular bioresource management.
W7223244670.title: Optimizing biomass-derived compost systems for reduced greenhouse gas emissions and improved nutrient recovery

W7223251430.abstract: Abstract This study investigated the removal of long- and short-chain per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) such as perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorobutanoic acid (PFBA) using alfalfa-derived biochar produced at different pyrolysis temperatures (300–900 °C). Increasing pyrolysis temperature substantially altered the physicochemical properties of the biochars, resulting in higher surface area, higher fixed carbon content, lower O/C and H/C ratios, and more condensed carbon structures. Among the tested materials, the biochar produced at 900 °C (AF900) showed the highest adsorption performance for both PFOA (0.39417 mg/g BC) and PFBA (0.0972 mg/g BC). Adsorption was strongly pH-dependent, with the highest removal observed at pH 3.0, and PFOA consistently showed much greater adsorption than PFBA. Possible mechanisms may include electrostatic, hydrophobic, and π–π interactions. The batch adsorption studies indicated that PFOA was better fitted to the pseudo-second-order and Freundlich models, and PFBA to the Elovich and Temkin models, while the adsorption of PFOA and PFBA followed endothermic reactions. The reusability experiment for AF900 showed a gradual decrease in regeneration efficiency over three cycles for PFOA and PFBA, with a relatively higher decrease for PFBA. Adsorption of PFOA and PFBA on AF900 in groundwater was lower than that in DI water, although increasing the loading rate of AF900 substantially improved PFAS removal in groundwater. Overall, AF900 was the best-performing material for adsorption of PFOA and PFBA among the alfalfa-derived biochars prepared at various temperatures in this study, whereas its removal performance in groundwater needs to be further studied.

W7223257608.abstract: This study presents a multimodal characterization of Methylosinus sp. strain C49 (MC49), a Type II methanotroph, to establish a reproducible workflow for methane mitigation and bioplastic polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) production. Cryopreserved cultures exhibited measurable growth by day 10, peaking at OD₆₀₀ 0.357 by day 14. Fluorescence microscopy identified SYBR Green I combined with SlowFade™ Diamond as optimal for cell visualization, while PCR-RFLP confirmed genetic purity across subcultures, storage methods, and environmental conditions, with minor changes after prolonged starvation. This integrated approach provides a reliable framework for methanotroph-based biotechnological applications and underscores critical considerations for culture maintenance, imaging, and molecular validation.

W7223266291.abstract: Wound infection caused by multidrug-resistant bacteria such as Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) presents a significant global health challenge, especially in the development of effective wound dressings. In this study, shrimp shell waste was utilized as a sustainable source for nanochitosan synthesis, offering a novel approach to biomedical material development. Electrospinning was used to fabricate polylactic acid (PLA)-based nanofiber membranes incorporating the synthesized nanochitosan. The resulting PLA-nanochitosan nanofibers exhibited uniform morphology with an average fiber diameter of 215.3 ± 38.9 nm, as characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy confirmed the successful incorporation of nanochitosan into the PLA matrix through the identification of functional group interactions. Antibacterial testing against MRSA using the agar diffusion method revealed a significant inhibition zone with an average diameter of 13.7 ± 0.5 mm, indicating potent antimicrobial activity. These findings demonstrate that shrimp shell-derived nanochitosan can enhance the antibacterial performance of PLA nanofibers, suggesting promising application in antimicrobial wound dressings and the valorization of seafood waste into high-value biomedical products.

W7223266860.abstract: Anthropogenic climate change is driving a fundamental destabilization of global climate systems, transitioning historical norms toward a regime characterized by extreme hydrological events, including prolonged droughts and severe flooding. These acute “pulse” disturbances exert severe physiological shocks on the soil microbiome, a critical biological engine responsible for global biogeochemical cycling, greenhouse gas dynamics, and macroscopic ecosystem resilience. Severe drought dismantles microbial communities through intense osmotic stress and restricted substrate diffusion, leading to widespread cellular lysis, significantly reducing microbial biomass, and suppressing the catalytic efficiency of extracellular enzymes. Conversely, extreme flooding plunges the highly heterogeneous soil matrix into rapid anoxia, triggering predictable taxonomic successions, the accumulation of phytotoxins. Furthermore, extreme flooding and subsequent water-table fluctuations drive profound shifts in carbon preservation mechanisms, governed by the “Enzyme Latch” (during persistent anoxia) and the “Iron Gate” (driven by redox changes during subsequent drainage) hypotheses. The violent, rapid transition between these extremes drought abruptly followed by severe rainfall induces the “Birch Effect,” causing a massive, transient pulse of soil respiration that drastically reduces microbial Carbon Use Efficiency (CUE) and accelerates the depletion of ancient carbon pools. To widen ecosystem tolerance thresholds and accelerate recovery from these pulse disturbances, this review evaluates the implementation of Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA) interventions, specifically highlighting the synergistic integration of biochar and continuous cover cropping. Rather than completely mitigating extreme physical forces, these targeted land management strategies buffer mild-to-moderate moisture extremes, provide structural refugia to preserve baseline microbial functionality, and align with global sustainability initiatives to secure more climate-resilient terrestrial ecosystems.
W7223266860.title: Impact of extreme hydrological events on soil microbiome dynamics and ecosystem resilience
